prompt: In a SOAP 1.1 request over HTTP, where is the operation named?
hint: Every request goes to the same address with the same method.

choices.text: In the path, as /invoice/IssueInvoice
choices.why: The service has one address, /invoice, for every operation.

choices.text: In the HTTP method
choices.why: The method is POST for every operation, so it cannot tell them apart.

choices.text: In SOAPAction and the Body's first element
choices.why: Right. The header names it for the server's routing, and the Body holds it with its arguments.

choices.text: In the envelope's Header element
choices.why: The Header carries signatures, tokens and trace ids, and is optional.

prompt: A SOAP 1.1 service answers HTTP 500. What does the status alone tell a tester?
hint: Look at the faultcode before deciding who failed.

choices.text: That the service crashed while handling the request
choices.why: A crash is one cause; a client mistake gets the same 500 in SOAP 1.1.

choices.text: That the request was malformed
choices.why: That is one cause, and the status cannot say which; the faultcode does.

choices.text: That a fault follows, and nothing about whose
choices.why: Right. SOAP 1.1 answers every fault with 500; soap:Client or soap:Server carries the blame.

choices.text: That the service speaks SOAP 1.2 and not 1.1
choices.why: 1.2 also uses 500 for receiver faults; the status says nothing about the version.

prompt: Match each part of a SOAP message to what it holds.
hint: One is optional, one is compulsory, one only appears when something went wrong.

pairs.right: the outermost element, whose namespace gives the version
optional: a signature, a token, a trace id
compulsory: the operation or its answer
the error, with who is to blame

right_distractors: the address the message is sent to

prompt: Why does the lesson give you a stand-in rather than sending you to the NF-e homologation environment?
hint: What does homologation still ask for?

choices.text: Homologation issues real fiscal documents
choices.why: It exists so that an invoice there has no fiscal value.

choices.text: Even homologation needs a company's digital certificate
choices.why: Right. A student's laptop has neither the registration nor the certificate.

choices.text: The NF-e services moved to REST and JSON
choices.why: The lesson describes them as SOAP with signed XML.

choices.text: curl cannot send a SOAP envelope to a real service
choices.why: Section 05 shows curl sends an envelope like any other body.

prompt: A bank's app talks JSON to its backend, and the backend calls a SOAP core system. Where is a tester of the app's API most likely to meet SOAP?
hint: Who sends the envelopes?

choices.text: In the phone's traffic, as envelopes the app sends
choices.why: The app sends JSON; the envelopes leave the backend.

choices.text: Nowhere: the JSON layer hides it from every test
choices.why: Its faults still decide whether the JSON call succeeds, so a test meets them.

choices.text: Behind the API, as a dependency
choices.why: Right. Its answers decide the JSON one, and what the backend does with a fault is a test.

choices.text: In the app's screens, which draw the XML
choices.why: Screens draw what the backend sent, and that is JSON.

prompt: Put the parts of a WSDL 1.1 document in the order the lesson reads them, from the address to the exact shapes.
hint: Bottom up.

prompt: Which request breaks the WSDL's own types, before any rule written in the service's code?
hint: Read the types part, not the code.

choices.text: A buyerTaxId of three digits
choices.why: The schema calls it a string and nothing more; the 11-digit rule is only in the code.

choices.text: An amountCents of 0
choices.why: Right. positiveInteger starts at 1, so 0 is invalid by the contract itself.

choices.text: An orderId of ord-1001 with an extra Header element in the envelope
choices.why: The Header is optional and outside the operation's types; this request is valid.

choices.text: An amountCents of 19500 for three seats
choices.why: 19500 is a positive integer, which is what the type asks.

prompt: The rule that buyerTaxId has 11 digits lives in the service's code and not in its WSDL. Why is that worth raising with whoever owns the contract?
hint: Who builds requests from the WSDL, and what do they know?

choices.text: Because a rule in the code is never enforced
choices.why: It is enforced: section 05 got a soap:Client fault for a short tax id.

choices.text: Because XML Schema has no way to say that a string holds exactly eleven digits
choices.why: It has: a pattern facet on the string would say it, so the gap is a choice.

choices.text: Because clients built from the WSDL will send values the code refuses
choices.why: Right. The contract promises a string, the code demands 11 digits, and only a run finds out.

choices.text: Because SoapUI refuses to send any value the WSDL's schema does not describe
choices.why: SoapUI sends what you type; its Schema Compliance assertion checks replies.

prompt: Why does the lesson send the envelope with --data-binary rather than -d?
hint: What does -d do to a file's line breaks?

choices.text: -d cannot read its body from a file
choices.why: -d reads a file with @ too; it strips the line breaks.

choices.text: It sends the file byte for byte
choices.why: Right. -d strips line breaks, which a signed document does not survive.

choices.text: It sets the content-type to text/xml for you
choices.why: The lesson sets content-type itself with -H; --data-binary does not.

choices.text: -d would send the request as a GET to the service
choices.why: -d sends a POST, as --data-binary does.

prompt: What HTTP status did the stand-in give to the envelope labelled application/soap+xml?
hint: It refused before reading the envelope.

prompt: Which of these are defects in the stand-in's answer to the envelope without amountCents?
hint: Two of them; one thing that looks wrong is SOAP 1.1's rule.

choices.text: The faultcode is soap:Server for a client's mistake
choices.why: Right. The request broke the contract, so soap:Client was due.

choices.text: The HTTP status is 500
choices.why: SOAP 1.1 answers every fault with 500; the short tax id got it too, correctly.

choices.text: The faultstring repeats an internal JavaScript error
choices.why: Right. It tells a stranger what the service is written in and nothing about the request.

choices.text: The answer is an envelope, not plain text
choices.why: A fault is meant to be an envelope with a Fault in its Body.

prompt: The short tax id got HTTP 500 and soap:Client. Is the 500 a defect?
hint: Lesson 1's rule was about REST.

choices.text: Yes: a client's mistake must get a 4xx, as lesson 1 said
choices.why: That holds for REST; SOAP 1.1 has its own rule for faults.

choices.text: Yes: SOAP 1.1 wants 400 for Client faults
choices.why: 400 for a sender fault is SOAP 1.2's binding; 1.1 uses 500 for all.

choices.text: No: 500 means it was accepted with a warning
choices.why: 500 means a fault follows; nothing was accepted.

choices.text: No: every SOAP 1.1 fault is a 500, whoever is to blame
choices.why: Right. soap:Client says the request was wrong, which is the correct answer.

prompt: xmllint --xpath '//invoiceNumber' prints "XPath set is empty" although the element is in the reply. Why?
hint: Look at the xmlns on IssueInvoiceResponse.

choices.text: // searches only the children of the root
choices.why: // searches the whole document at any depth.

choices.text: The element is called InvoiceNumber, with a capital I, not invoiceNumber
choices.why: The reply writes invoiceNumber; the name matches.

choices.text: It is namespaced, and a bare name means no namespace
choices.why: Right. The default xmlns puts every element inside it in urn:example:invoice:v1.

choices.text: xmllint reads only the first line of what arrives on its input
choices.why: It reads the whole document; the call printed the faultcode from deeper lines.

prompt: The XPath function ___() gives an element's tag without its prefix, so it matches the invoice number whatever namespace it is in.
hint: The lesson wrote it inside square brackets.

prompt: What exit status did bash soap/check.sh give, the number a pipeline stops on?
hint: echo $? printed it after the run.

prompt: Why does //faultcode find the fault's code when //invoiceNumber found nothing?
hint: Which elements does SOAP 1.1 put in a namespace?

choices.text: Because its value, soap:Client, carries a prefix
choices.why: The prefix in the value is text; XPath matches on the element's own name.

choices.text: Because SOAP 1.1 leaves faultcode in no namespace
choices.why: Right. A bare name means no namespace, and faultcode has none.

choices.text: Because xmllint treats faults as a special case
choices.why: xmllint knows nothing of SOAP; it reads XML.

choices.text: Because faults are smaller documents, so XPath reaches every element in them
choices.why: Size changes nothing; // reaches any depth in both.

prompt: Which SoapUI assertion checks every element of a reply against the types in the WSDL?
hint: The one with no line in soap/check.sh.

choices.text: XPath Match
choices.why: It checks one expression against one value.

choices.text: Not SOAP Fault
choices.why: It checks only that the reply is not a fault.

choices.text: Contains
choices.why: It looks for a piece of text anywhere in the reply.

choices.text: Schema Compliance
choices.why: Right. It reads the WSDL's XML Schema and checks the whole reply against it.

prompt: Match each check in soap/check.sh to the SoapUI assertion that does the same job.
hint: The table in the section.

pairs.left: boolean of the Fault element is false
the negative cases expect a fault

prompt: In a SoapUI project made from the WSDL, why does nobody type the SOAPAction header?
hint: Which part of the WSDL holds the action?

choices.text: Because SoapUI speaks SOAP 1.2, which has no such header
choices.why: SoapUI speaks the version the binding declares, and this one is 1.1.

choices.text: It comes from the binding
choices.why: Right. The soapAction of each operation is in the binding, and SoapUI reads it.

choices.text: Because the stand-in ignores the header anyway
choices.why: It requires it: a request without one got a soap:Client fault.

choices.text: Because the MockService adds it
choices.why: A MockService answers requests; it does not send them.

prompt: boxoffice calls the invoice service after each payment, retries every soap:Server fault three times, and gives up at once on soap:Client. With the defect you found, what happens to a call sent without an amount?
hint: Which faultcode does that request get?

choices.text: It fails at once, because a missing field is the client's mistake
choices.why: That is what should happen; the defect makes the service answer soap:Server instead.

choices.text: It succeeds on a retry, since server faults pass
choices.why: The same envelope throws the same error every time; nothing changes between tries.

choices.text: It is retried three times, failing each time
choices.why: Right. The fault blames the service, so the caller retries a request that cannot succeed.

choices.text: It is invoiced with an amount of 0
choices.why: No invoice is issued; the service faults before it gets that far.

prompt: A colleague's SOAP tests assert only the HTTP status, 200 for valid requests and 500 for invalid ones. Which defect of this lesson would pass them?
hint: Two faults with the same status and different blame.

choices.text: A valid order answered with a fault
choices.why: A fault is a 500, so the test expecting 200 would fail and catch it.

choices.text: A missing amount answered soap:Server
choices.why: Right. Both faults are 500, so only the faultcode tells the defect apart.

choices.text: A short tax id that was accepted with an invoice number
choices.why: An accepted request is a 200, so the test expecting 500 would catch it.

choices.text: None: with SOAP, the status code carries the whole verdict
choices.why: In SOAP 1.1 every fault shares one status, so the status cannot carry the verdict.

prompt: Another service answers an envelope missing a required field with HTTP 400 and the fault code env:Sender. What does a tester conclude?
hint: Which version uses Sender, and what status does it give a sender fault?

choices.text: Correct: SOAP 1.2 sends sender faults as 400
choices.why: Right. Sender and 400 are 1.2's answer to a request that was wrong.

choices.text: A defect, because a SOAP fault must be 500
choices.why: That is 1.1's rule; env:Sender says this service speaks 1.2.

choices.text: A defect: the code should read soap:Client
choices.why: Client is 1.1's name; 1.2 renamed it Sender.

choices.text: The service is a REST API that happens to return XML
choices.why: env:Sender inside a Fault is SOAP 1.2's vocabulary.

prompt: You are handed the address of a SOAP service you have never seen. Put the steps of a first test session in order.
hint: Each step needs something the one before it found.
items: read the binding for the version and each SOAPAction
read the types for each field and its type
send one valid envelope and assert the reply
send envelopes that break one rule each and assert the faultcode
